sections.h2: Where do I find McLennan County property records?
sections.html:
Deeds and other real property records for McLennan County are kept by the County Clerk in Waco, in the McLennan County Records Building at 215 N 5th Street, Room 223, Waco, TX 76701. The clerk's phone line is 254-757-5078, and the office is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., except county holidays.

The same office is the custodian of liens, hospital liens, cattle brands, assumed name certificates and marriage licenses, and it is clerk of the probate court and the commissioners' court. For a seller, that means one counter holds most of the paper a title company will ask about. Staff cannot give legal advice, so questions about what a document means go to an attorney or to a legal aid group.

Texas law makes the county clerk the county recorder, and deeds are filed in the county where the land sits. A house anywhere in McLennan County is recorded here, even if the owner lives somewhere else.

sections.h2: How far back do the McLennan County records go?
sections.html:
The clerk's records start in 1849 and run to the present, split between bound volumes and an electronic system. The county's page says everything recorded from January 1, 1996 forward is searchable online and on public workstations in the clerk's office.

McLennan County Clerk record coverage (source: McLennan County Clerk pages)
PeriodWhere the record lives
1849 through 1995Manual records in book volumes at the clerk's office
December 1968 through December 1995Deed and deed of trust volumes, listed among items reachable on office workstations
April 1969 through December 1995Mechanic's lien volumes
September 1990 through December 1995Deeds, deeds of trust and mechanic's liens added to electronic records
January 1, 1996 to the presentOfficial Public Records, searchable online

The middle rows overlap because the county lists its older material in more than one place. If your deed was recorded before 1996, call the clerk before you drive over and ask which format holds it.

sections.h2: How do I search the McLennan County records?
sections.html:
Search by name. The clerk states that McLennan County does not index by legal description, so you need the grantor or the grantee, meaning the seller or the buyer on the deed you want.

  • Use the Online Records Search linked from the clerk's Official Public Records page for anything recorded since 1996.
  • Use the public workstations in the Records Building for older volumes and for anything the online tool does not show.
  • Do not expect to find a property survey. In Texas surveys cannot be recorded on their own, so the county has one only when it was attached as an exhibit to another recorded document, which is rare.

Write down the book, volume and page or the instrument number for every document you find. Your title company can then pull the exact copies instead of searching again.

sections.h2: What does McLennan County require to record a deed?
sections.html:
The clerk publishes a short list of standard requirements, and a document that misses one of them is returned, not recorded. The office also warns that it cannot advise on legal matters and will only record completed documents that meet the filing rules.

  • The property must be in McLennan County, and any document about real property needs a legal description.
  • Every signature must be an original and must be proved, acknowledged or sworn to under Texas law.
  • Only original documents are taken, with the exception of certified copies from another government agency.
  • The document needs a heading that names its type, must be in English, and must carry a return address.
  • A deed must also show a grantee address, which the clerk says is used for tax purposes.
  • Accepted payment: cash, cashier's or business checks, money orders, personal checks, and Visa, MasterCard or American Express.

The clerk's FAQ adds two practical points. There is no notary at the counter to acknowledge your signature, so have the deed notarized beforehand, and the recorded original is mailed back the next business day.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed in McLennan County?
sections.html:
Texas sets recording fees by statute, and the Texas Courts county clerk manual lists the base structure: $5.00 for the first page, $4.00 for each added page, and $0.25 for each name past five that must be indexed. Separate county fees add up to $10 for records management, up to $10 for a records archive, and $2.00 for records technology.

A deed that leaves out the grantee's mailing address can pick up an extra $25. The McLennan County Clerk posts its own Recording Fee Schedule as a PDF on its Official Public Records page, so use that schedule for the exact total, and ask the clerk's office or your title company to confirm the amount before you send a check.

sections.h2: What if the records show a lien, an old foreclosure or an unknown heir?
sections.html:
A title company searches these records before closing, so anything unresolved will show up at that stage. Common finds are a paid-off mortgage with no recorded release, a hospital lien, a mechanic's lien, or a deed signed by a relative who has since died.

  • Unpaid property tax travels with the house. McLennan County says taxes are delinquent if not paid before February 1 of the following year, and tax sales are held online through GovEase.
  • Trustee sales for foreclosures are run by the trustee named on each notice, not by the clerk. The clerk's page says they take place on the outside steps of the McLennan County Courthouse at 501 Washington Ave., usually starting at 10 a.m., with notices viewable at the clerk's office.
  • Inherited property can be sorted out through the probate court, whose case files the County Clerk maintains. Texas also allows an affidavit of heirship recorded with the clerk, though the State Law Library notes that no law forces anyone to accept it.

When a record problem is holding up a sale, a buyer who purchases as-is and works through the title company may be able to handle the cleanup as part of closing.

sections.h2: Who appraises McLennan County property, and when is a protest due?
sections.html:
The McLennan Central Appraisal District, at 315 S 26th Street, Waco, TX 76710, sets the value that the county and the other taxing units use. Owners whose market value rose by at least $1,000 receive a Notice of Appraised Value each spring, and the district says the protest deadline is May 15 or 30 days after the notice is mailed, whichever is later.

After a protest is filed, the owner can meet informally with an appraiser, and if there is no agreement the case goes to the Appraisal Review Board. The district's page says online protests for most residential property open on April 10 and run through May 15. Homestead exemptions are filed on Form 50-114 with the appraisal district, generally by April 30.

Deed records do not carry the tax bill, so a buyer should ask the McLennan County Tax Office for the current account status. Texas puts a tax lien on property each January 1, and the owner on that date is liable for that year's tax.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about McLennan County?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau estimated McLennan County at 272,020 people on July 1, 2025, up from 260,579 counted in the 2020 census and 234,906 in 2010. The county covers 1,036.66 square miles of land, which works out to 251.4 people per square mile in 2020.

Housing figures for 2020 through 2024 show an owner-occupied rate of 61.8% and a median owner-occupied home value of $243,600. Median gross rent was $1,173, median household income was $66,643, and the county had 97,338 households with an average of 2.64 people each. The Census Bureau counted 1,442 building permits in 2025 and 112,290 housing units as of mid-2025.

Ask the title company to compare the recorded deed, the tax account and the seller's name early in the sale, so a mismatch surfaces before the closing date.

faqs.q: Can I search McLennan County deeds by property address?
faqs.a: No, the clerk says McLennan County does not index by legal description, so you need the name of the grantor or the grantee. Use the Online Records Search for 1996 and later, or the public workstations in the Records Building for older volumes.

faqs.q: Where is the McLennan County Clerk's office?
faqs.a: It is on the second floor of the McLennan County Records Building at 215 N 5th Street, Room 223, Waco, TX 76701. The phone is 254-757-5078, and hours are Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., except holidays.

faqs.q: Can the clerk's office notarize my deed?
faqs.a: No. The clerk's FAQ says there is no notary at the office to acknowledge documents, so sign before a notary elsewhere and bring the original, since copies are not accepted.

faqs.q: Does the County Clerk run the foreclosure sale?
faqs.a: No. The clerk's page states that trustee sales are conducted by the trustee named on each notice. They take place on the outside steps in front of the courthouse at 501 Washington Ave., Waco, and the notices can be read at the clerk's office.

faqs.q: How do I find out whether back taxes are owed on a McLennan County house?
faqs.a: Ask the McLennan County Tax Office, which bills the tax and says it is delinquent if unpaid before February 1 of the following year. A title company will also show unpaid tax on its commitment before closing.
